title: Alexander the Great Biography Wins £50,000 Baillie Gifford Non-Fiction Prize
excerpt: Durham historian Edmund Richardson's 'Alexander: God, King, Man' is the first ancient-history book to win the prize since 1999, beating a shortlist that included Patrick Radden Keefe and Anand Gopal.
body:
• Edmund Richardson, a 44-year-old historian at the University of Durham, has won the £50,000 Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction for "Alexander: God, King, Man."
  • It is the first ancient-history title to win the prize since the award was launched in 1999, and the first major prize of Richardson's career.
  • The book draws on more than a decade of research across four continents and new translations of sources from 12 ancient languages.
  • The six-book shortlist, chosen from more than 350 eligible titles, included Patrick Radden Keefe's "London Falling" and Anand Gopal's "Days of Love and Rage."

An "immersive" biography of Alexander the Great has won the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction, Britain's most prestigious award for the genre. Edmund Richardson, a professor of history at the University of Durham, was named the winner for "Alexander: God, King, Man" at a ceremony in central London, receiving £50,000 (about $67,000). It is the first time a book on ancient history has won the prize since it was launched in 1999.

A decade in the archives, from Egypt to Afghanistan

The book is based on more than a decade of research across four continents and includes new translations of sources from 12 ancient languages; Richardson's research took him from the catacombs of Egypt to the passes of Afghanistan. It follows Alexander from his accession at 20 to a debt-ridden Macedonian throne and a restless army, through his transformation into a conqueror worshipped as a living god, to his death in Babylon aged 32.

Richardson, 44, called the win "one of the greatest honours of my life." "To tell you the absolute truth, I still don't believe it," he said in a statement. "When you write about the ancient world, when you write about stories over 2000 years old, you don't expect people to pay attention."

"Alexander: God, King, Man is non-fiction writing at its very best: a book that, like its subject, can't stop pressing onward. It's blockbuster history with page-turning narrative pull."

— Kirsty Lang, Chair of Judges, Baillie Gifford Prize

Why the judges chose it

Announcing the winner, chair of judges Kirsty Lang said the book "combines the use of new technology and recent archaeological discoveries to tell the story of an extraordinary leader who conquered an empire stretching from Ancient Greece to the Indian subcontinent." The panel included Waterstones head of books Bea Carvalho, writer Tiffany Jenkins, the Spectator's literary editor Sam Leith, New York Times editor Ravi Mattu, and novelist Elif Shafak.

The winner was selected from more than 350 eligible books published between November 1, 2025, and October 31, 2026. The six-title shortlist Richardson beat included Patrick Radden Keefe's "London Falling," Anand Gopal's "Days of Love and Rage: A Story of Revolution," and Nicholas Boggs's "Baldwin: A Love Story."

The India thread

Alexander's story ends, geographically, at the edge of India: his campaigns reached the Punjab, the easternmost extent of the empire the judges described. For readers in India and the diaspora, the prize is a reminder that the ancient world's most retold life still turns on sources and sites across South and Central Asia — and that, 2,300 years later, a fresh telling of it can still beat the biggest names in modern non-fiction.
